---
title: "Will AI take your job? Workforce and economics"
subtitle: "AIM-3 · AIM-7 · about 90 minutes"
---

::: {.callout-note title="What you'll learn"}
By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

1. State what was predicted for radiology in 2016, what the primary data show
   happened through 2026, and why "he was just early" is an inadequate reading.
2. Apply a four-factor framework, task decomposition, real-world generalization,
   liability, and demand, to the specialty you are entering, and grade a
   chatbot's forecast about that specialty with the same four factors.
3. Use the mammography computer-aided detection precedent to explain why
   adoption of a tool and improvement in outcomes are separate questions.
4. Explain why a tool can reduce work inside one organization while raising
   cost across the system, and describe the "bot wars" dynamic.
5. Read the Bureau of Labor Statistics projections for three health-information
   occupations and explain why adjacent jobs move in opposite directions.
6. Name the most automatable *task* in your intended specialty, estimate what
   fraction of the job it is, and say what would change your estimate.
:::

**Time.** About 25 minutes of reading, 20 minutes of watching, 35 minutes of
doing, and 10 minutes for the check and the standing question. You need one
general-purpose chatbot (your institutional ChatGPT Edu or Microsoft Copilot
account is enough) and a browser. Nothing installs, nothing asks for a phone
number, and nothing in this chapter touches a patient.

## The year everyone says radiology is over

It is September of your fourth year. You have your radiology letters, your
program list, and a spreadsheet of interview dates. At a family dinner, an
uncle who reads about technology asks why you would go into the one specialty
the "godfather of AI" said should stop training people. He has the quote on
his phone: in 2016 Geoffrey Hinton, who would later share a Nobel Prize for the
neural networks that make modern AI work, told a Toronto audience that people
should *stop training radiologists now*, because within five years deep
learning would obviously do the job better.

::: {.vendor-slide}
<div class="brand">Machine Learning and the Market for Intelligence · Toronto · 2016</div>
<h4>"People should stop training radiologists now."</h4>
<div class="stats">
<div class="stat"><b>5 yrs</b><span>until deep learning "obviously" outperforms radiologists</span></div>
<div class="stat"><b>0</b><span>new radiologists needed</span></div>
</div>
<div class="foot">A confident forecast about a whole job, made by the person best placed to make it</div>
<div class="fine">Illustrative rendering of a public remark for this chapter; not the speaker's slide. The quote is real and is linked in the Watch section.</div>
:::

Your uncle is not wrong that Hinton said it, and he is not wrong that Hinton
knows more about deep learning than anyone at the table. The question is what
happened next, and whether the way the prediction failed tells you anything
about the job you are about to spend a decade training for. You are not in
radiology? The same uncle has a version of the question for every specialty,
and so does every chatbot. This chapter is about how to answer it with
something other than a feeling.

## Why this matters

You are making a thirty-year bet with a spreadsheet and a gut feeling. Nobody
can tell you how your specialty will look in 2056. But the most confident,
most credentialed prediction that a medical job would disappear has now run
its course, and it failed in a specific, instructive way. A forecast that
fails is more useful than one that has not been tested yet, because you can
take it apart and see which assumptions broke.

There is a second reason, and it is the one your co-residents will not think
about. The people whose jobs are already changing are not physicians. Medical
transcription is shrinking; medical coding is growing; both sit ten feet from
where you will work. A resident who understands why is more useful to the team
than one who is merely relieved about their own position.

## The idea

### What actually happened

The prediction was five years. Ten years on, the National Resident Matching
Program's own tables tell the story in @fig-match. Diagnostic radiology offered
more advanced (PGY-2) positions in 2026 than in any of the previous four
years, and filled 98.4 percent of them; 1,741 applicants ranked the specialty
for 1,083 positions.[^nrmp]

[^nrmp]: NRMP, *Results and Data: 2026 Main Residency Match* (May 2026),
    Tables 1A, 3 and 7A, read from the
    [primary PDF](https://www.nrmp.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Main_Match_Results_and_Data-2026.pdf)
    on 2026-09-07. The figure shows advanced (PGY-2) diagnostic radiology
    positions; a further 156 categorical PGY-1 positions were offered in 2026
    and 148 filled.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-match
%%| fig-cap: "Diagnostic radiology advanced (PGY-2) positions offered and filled in the Main Residency Match, 2022 to 2026. Redrawn from NRMP Results and Data 2026, Tables 3 and 7A. Positions rose every year; the gap between the bars is the number unfilled."
xychart-beta
    title "Diagnostic radiology PGY-2 positions, NRMP Main Match"
    x-axis [2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026]
    y-axis "Positions" 900 --> 1120
    bar "Offered" [997, 1006, 1017, 1057, 1083]
    bar "Filled" [996, 1006, 1016, 1042, 1066]
```

The rest of the picture points the same way. The Neiman Health Policy
Institute counted 37,482 radiologists serving Medicare patients in 2023 and
projected a workforce 25.7 percent larger by 2055 even if residency positions
stop growing, and 40.3 percent larger if they keep growing [@pmid:39952776].
Attrition, the rate at which working radiologists leave clinical practice,
more than doubled between 2014 and 2022, from 1.1 to 2.5 percent a year, and
the authors frame that as a contributor to a *shortage*, not a surplus
[@pmid:41031940]. Doximity's 2026 compensation survey put average diagnostic
radiology compensation at $609,684 for 2025, up 6.6 percent in a year when
physician pay overall rose about 2 percent.[^dox]

[^dox]: Doximity, *2026 Physician Compensation Report*, covering 2025;
    <https://www.doximity.com/reports/physician-compensation-report/2026>.
    The module this chapter is built from quotes the prior year's figure,
    $571,749, up 7.5 percent. The two are different survey years, not
    competing estimates; quote one with its year.

::: {.callout-note title="The subspecialty exception"}
One number keeps this from being blanket reassurance. Counting radiologists
who bill at least half their work for children, the pediatric radiology
workforce shrank from 2,190 in 2016 to 2,032 in 2023, from 6.4 to 4.6 percent
of all radiologists, while imaging demand rose [@pmid:40923948]. That is not
automation; it is the labor market of a subspecialty moving independently of
its parent. A student choosing a fellowship is making a finer-grained bet than
the headline numbers describe.
:::

In May 2025 Hinton told the *New York Times* that he had spoken too broadly in
2016, that he had meant image analysis rather than the job, and that he now
expects most image interpretation to be done by "a combination of A.I. and a
radiologist."[^hinton] Here is the prediction as it was covered when it was
fresh, and as it reads now.

[^hinton]: Steve Lohr, "Your A.I. Radiologist Will Not Be With You Soon,"
    *New York Times*, 14 May 2025. The direct quotation is as reported by
    [AuntMinnie](https://www.auntminnie.com/imaging-informatics/artificial-intelligence/article/15746014/hinton-acknowledges-mistake-in-predicting-ai-replacement-of-radiologists),
    because the original is paywalled. The module this chapter is built from
    dated the interview May 2026; the correct date is May 2025.

:::

Read the fourth clipping twice. "More positions than ever" and "applicant
pool declines" are in the same headline. Students are hearing the prediction
and acting on it even as the labor market moves the other way; that is a
harm the prediction did, and it fell on the people who believed it.

### Why "he was just early" is not enough

The lazy reading is that the timeline slipped. Hinton's own 2025 correction is
more interesting: he says he meant a task, image analysis, and said a job. That
is not a timing error. The prediction failed for four structural reasons, and
each one is a question you can ask about any specialty.

**1. Task decomposition.** A job is automatable to the extent that it breaks
into tasks a machine can be measured on. In 2012, observers followed fourteen
staff radiologists through their workdays at three hospitals with a stopwatch
and found that 36.4 percent of their time went to interpreting images
[@pmid:23763878]. The rest was protocolling requests, supervising studies,
procedures, consulting with other physicians, and direct patient care
(@fig-workday). A tool that read every image perfectly would leave nearly
two-thirds of the day untouched, and it would not sign the report.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-workday
%%| fig-cap: "How fourteen hospital radiologists spent their time in 2012, from a time-and-motion study at three Vancouver hospitals. Redrawn from the abstract of Dhanoa et al. (2013): 36.4 percent image interpretation, 43.8 percent noninterpretive clinical tasks; the remaining categories are derived from the reported 87.7 percent total clinical productivity."
pie showData
    title "A radiologist's day (percent of time)"
    "Image interpretation" : 36.4
    "Noninterpretive clinical work" : 43.8
    "Other clinical" : 7.5
    "Nonclinical" : 12.3
```

**2. Real-world generalization.** A model that beats radiologists on a
benchmark has beaten them on one dataset. When deep-learning models for
pneumonia on chest radiographs were trained at one hospital system and tested
at another, performance dropped, and the models could tell which hospital an
image came from with better than 99.9 percent accuracy, which means they had
learned the scanner as much as the disease [@pmid:30399157]. Radiology also
carries most of the regulatory weight: of 903 AI-enabled devices the FDA had
authorized by August 2024, 692 (76.6 percent) were radiology devices, and
clinical performance studies were reported for only 55.9 percent of all
devices, with 2.4 percent randomized [@pmid:40305017]. Hundreds of cleared
tools, and no measured displacement of labor. The most-read explanation of why
is Deena Mousa's essay "AI isn't replacing radiologists" (October 2025), which
also reports that 38 percent of 2024-cleared models that disclosed their test
sites used data from a single hospital
[VERIFY: 38% single-site figure is Mousa's reading of the JAMA Netw Open analysis; not in that paper's abstract]{.verify}.[^mousa]

[^mousa]: Deena Mousa, "AI isn't replacing radiologists," *Understanding AI*,
    1 October 2025, <https://www.understandingai.org/p/ai-isnt-replacing-radiologists>.
    The best single reading if you want the whole argument in one sitting.

**3. Liability and regulatory structure.** Someone signs the read. Malpractice
law measures the physician, not the model, and the joint statement of the
American, Canadian, European, Australasian, and North American radiology
societies describes current tools as augmenting rather than replacing the
radiologist's interpretation, with autonomous function treated as a separate
question needing its own evidence [@pmid:38276923]. The device boundary and
who is liable when a tool is wrong belong to the ethics and regulation
chapter; the point here is only that the structure is designed to keep a human
in the loop, and a design is slower to change than a benchmark.

**4. Demand.** Making a task cheaper does not obviously reduce the number of
people doing it. Economists call the pattern the Jevons paradox, after the
nineteenth-century observation that more efficient steam engines increased
coal consumption: cheaper imaging gets ordered more. The workforce projection
above assumes demand keeps growing at least as fast as supply
[VERIFY: Neiman demand projection of 17–27% growth in imaging, cited in the module, not retrieved this session]{.verify}.
The same paradox runs through the environmental-impact chapter, if you take
it: efficiency per unit and total consumption move in opposite directions
more often than intuition expects.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-four-factors
%%| fig-cap: "The four questions, in the order they usually settle an argument. A task that fails any one of them stays with the human; a job is the sum of its tasks."
flowchart TD
    T[Pick one task in the job] --> Q1{Can a machine be<br/>measured on it?}
    Q1 -- No --> H[Stays with the human]
    Q1 -- Yes --> Q2{Does it work at a hospital<br/>that did not build it?}
    Q2 -- Not shown --> H
    Q2 -- Yes --> Q3{Who signs, and who is<br/>liable when it is wrong?}
    Q3 -- The physician --> A[Assists the human]
    Q3 -- The tool --> Q4{Is demand capped?}
    Q4 -- No: more gets ordered --> M[More of the task, same people]
    Q4 -- Yes --> R[Fewer people do this task]
```

Groups working through this usually converge on the first question without
being told to. That convergence is worth noticing: most physician jobs
decompose badly, and the specialties that look most automatable from outside
are the ones whose perceptual core is most visible, not the ones where it is
the largest share of the work.

::: {.callout-important title="A concrete case where the habit gets the wrong answer"}
Ask your chatbot, "Will AI replace radiologists?" You will get a fluent,
balanced answer that mentions image analysis, workflow, and the human touch.
Now ask it for the fraction of a radiologist's day spent interpreting images,
with a source. Most models give a number without a source, or a source that
does not contain the number. The 2012 time-and-motion study above is one
paper with fourteen radiologists; a model that has not read it is guessing,
and a guess in a confident register is the whole failure mode this chapter is
about. You will do this properly in the Do block.
:::

### The precedent: mammography CAD

The closest historical rehearsal went further than most students expect.
Computer-aided detection (CAD) for screening mammography, software that marks
suspicious regions for the radiologist, was approved by the FDA in 1998 and
given a Medicare add-on payment in 2002. By the late 2000s it was used on
most screening mammograms in the United States at a cost of over $400 million
a year [@pmid:26414882]. It was, by adoption, a success.

Then the outcome data arrived. Across 429,345 mammograms at 43 facilities,
introducing CAD lowered specificity from 90.2 to 87.2 percent, raised the
biopsy rate by 19.7 percent, and did not significantly change the cancer
detection rate [@pmid:17409321]. A later analysis of 625,625 digital
mammograms found no improvement on any metric with CAD, and among radiologists
who read both with and without it, sensitivity was *lower* with CAD
[@pmid:26414882]. The Medicare add-on payment was eventually withdrawn
[VERIFY: year the CAD add-on was folded into the base mammography payment; secondary sources say 2018]{.verify}.
A technology was adopted at scale, generated extra procedures for patients, and
was paid out of existence.

The finding to sit with is smaller and worse. When readers were shown
mammograms with a deliberately high proportion of cases where the CAD marks
were wrong, their sensitivity fell compared with readers who had no computer
output at all, and it fell most on exactly the cancers the computer had missed
[@pmid:15354301]. The name for this is automation bias, the tendency to
over-rely on a machine's suggestion, and it has been documented across
aviation, decision support, and imaging [@pmid:21685142]. CAD did not replace
the radiologists. It made some of them worse. That is a different and more
troubling failure than the one everyone was worried about, and it is the
shape of the sepsis alert you will silence in your first month: a tool that is
wrong in a systematic way degrades the human rather than being caught by them.

Adoption and outcomes are separate questions. Objective 3 is that sentence.

### The economics the debate does not surface

Everything so far produces optimism about physician employment. This section
complicates it, because "your job survives" and "the system gets better or
cheaper" are different claims.

**Within the organization.** The critical appraisal chapter follows ambient
scribes through their evidence tiers. The five-system study of 8,581 clinicians
found scribe adopters spent 13.4 fewer minutes a day in the EHR and 16.0 fewer
on documentation, and delivered 0.49 more visits per week, while after-hours
EHR time did not change significantly [@pmid:41920565]. At UCSF, across 1,565
physicians and about 1.2 million ambulatory encounters, adopters billed 1.81
more relative value units (RVUs, the unit Medicare uses to price physician
work) per week, a 5.8 percent increase, saw 0.80 more encounters, and had no
rise in claim denials [@pmid:41511775]. Time saved became visits and RVUs.
That is real, it is what a hospital's finance office wants, and it is not cost
reduction.

**Across the system.** The Peterson Health Technology Institute, which takes no
vendor money, concluded in March 2025 that scribes probably reduce burnout but
show little evidence of financial return, and in April 2026 that
administrative AI reduces burden *inside* organizations while failing to lower
system-wide costs and possibly raising them.[^phti] The mechanism it names is
"bot wars": providers use AI to submit more prior-authorization requests and
code visits more intensively; payers use AI to process more denials and
"downcode" claims automatically; the volume of back-and-forth rises without
any clinical question being resolved faster. PHTI's April 2026 report also
records a system where Level 5 visit coding rose 5 percent after scribe
deployment, worth over $1,000 per provider per month, which is the UCSF
finding seen from the payer's side.

[^phti]: Peterson Health Technology Institute, *Adoption of AI in Healthcare
    Delivery Systems: Early Applications and Impacts* (March 2025) and
    *Administrative AI: Current Use and Potential Impact* (April 2026),
    <https://phti.org/administrative-ai-current-use-and-potential-impact/>.
    The "bot wars" phrase and the Level 5 coding example are as reported in
    trade coverage of the April 2026 report
    ([HIT Consultant](https://hitconsultant.net/2026/04/13/phti-report-ai-upcoding-trap-ambient-scribes-payer-downcoding/),
    13 April 2026); the report page itself was fetched but the phrase was not
    located in the summary text
    [VERIFY: "bot wars" wording against the full PHTI PDF]{.verify}.

**One number to refuse to simplify.** You will hear that "25 percent of health
care spending is administrative." That sentence blends three studies with
three denominators. Shrank and colleagues estimated total *waste* at $760 to
$935 billion, about 25 percent of spending, of which administrative complexity
is one of six categories [@pmid:31589283]. Himmelstein and colleagues found
administration to be 25.3 percent of *hospital* expenditures, the highest of
eight nations [@pmid:25201663]. Woolhandler and colleagues put administration
at $294.3 billion in 1999, 31.0 percent of expenditures *after exclusions*,
using the broadest definition in the literature [@pmid:12930930]. Three
numbers, three denominators. The habit of asking "percent of what?" outlasts
all three figures.

### The most useful single fact: the BLS contradiction

The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) publishes ten-year employment projections
for every occupation in its *Occupational Outlook Handbook*. Three of them sit
side by side in the medical records department (@fig-bls).

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-bls
%%| fig-cap: "Projected employment change, 2025 to 2035, for three health-information occupations. Redrawn from the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook pages for each occupation, read 2026-09-07. Same industry, same technology, opposite directions."
xychart-beta
    title "BLS projected employment change, 2025–2035 (percent)"
    x-axis ["Medical transcriptionists", "Medical records specialists", "Health information technologists"]
    y-axis "Percent change" -10 --> 20
    bar [-4, 8, 16]
```

| Occupation | 2025 jobs | Projected change, 2025–35 | BLS's stated reason |
|---|---|---|---|
| Medical transcriptionists | 42,000 | −4% | Speech recognition and natural language processing let physicians document in real time |
| Medical records specialists | 200,700 | +8% | Aging population, chronic disease, more coding for reimbursement; AI coding tools "may affect" demand |
| Health information technologists and medical registrars | 42,000 | +16% | Growing volume of electronic health information needing analysis and registry maintenance |

: The three projections, with the reason BLS gives for each. Read from the *Occupational Outlook Handbook* on 2026-09-07: [transcriptionists](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/medical-transcriptionists.htm), [records specialists](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/medical-records-and-health-information-technicians.htm), [health information technologists](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/health-information-technologists-and-medical-registrars.htm). BLS revises these every two years; the module this chapter is built from carried the 2024–34 figures (−5, +7, +15 percent) as unverified, and the 2025–35 revision replaced them while this chapter was being written. {#tbl-bls}

What distinguishes them is the four-factor framework applied to non-physician
work. Transcription decomposes into a single benchmarkable task, generalizes
well because speech is speech, has no signature attached, and its demand is
capped by the number of encounters. Coding and health-information work fail the
first test: the job is judgment about what a record means and what a payer
will accept, and the bot-wars dynamic above is *increasing* that work, not
removing it. The people whose jobs change first are your colleagues, and the
harm is not evenly distributed: transcription is lower-paid than the two
occupations that are growing, so the displaced workers are the ones with the
least cushion. The bias and equity chapter has the vocabulary for that,
harms of allocation, and it applies to labor as much as to diagnosis.

## Watch or listen

**First, the source (1 min 24 s).** "Geoff Hinton: On Radiology," Creative
Destruction Lab, YouTube, uploaded 24 November 2016.
<https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2HMPRXstSvQ>. Watch it cold. Notice how
specific the claim is, how confident the tone is, and that the argument is
entirely about image analysis. He is describing a task and forecasting a job.
That gap is the chapter.

**Then, the other side (watch the first 20 minutes).** "AIMI Grand Rounds:
Developing Clinically Useful AI for Radiology," Curtis Langlotz, Stanford AIMI,
YouTube, 30 January 2025, 59 min 37 s.
<https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WS9p0wFw7uY>. Langlotz is the radiologist
who wrote, in 2019, that AI will not replace radiologists but radiologists who
use AI will replace those who do not [@pmid:33937794]. Listen for what he
says makes a tool *clinically useful* as opposed to accurate, and for every
place where the obstacle he describes is one of the four factors rather than
model performance. Twenty minutes is enough for the exercise; the rest is a
good commute.

If you would rather read than watch, Mousa's essay in the footnote above
covers the same ground in about the same time.

## Do

::: {.callout-warning title="No patient information, and no classmate's data"}
Every prompt in this exercise is about a specialty, an occupation, or a
published number. None is about a patient, a rotation, or a person you know.
Your institutional chatbot account does not change the no-PHI rule, and free
tiers may use what you type to train the next model. The one thing you will
paste is a public government web page.
:::

### Part A: grade the model (10 minutes)

**Step 1.** Open your chatbot and ask, substituting your intended specialty
(or radiology if you are undecided):

> I am a fourth-year medical student choosing a specialty. Will AI replace
> `<specialty>` by 2036? Give me your best forecast and your reasoning.

**Step 2.** Grade the answer against the four factors. The question for each
row is not "did it mention this" but "did it give me something I could check."

```
Tool: ____________________   Specialty: ____________________

Factor              Mentioned?  Gave a checkable number or source?   Note
Task decomposition    Y / N        Y / N                             ______
Generalization        Y / N        Y / N                             ______
Liability/signature   Y / N        Y / N                             ______
Demand                Y / N        Y / N                             ______

Its forecast in one line: ______________________________________________
What fraction of the job did it say is automatable? ______  Source? Y / N
```

**Step 3.** Ask one follow-up:

> What fraction of a `<specialty>` physician's working time is spent on the
> task you think is most automatable? Give me the study you are relying on,
> with authors, journal, and year.

Search PubMed for whatever it gives you. If the study exists and contains the
number, note it. If it does not, you have just watched a confident forecast
rest on nothing, which is the lesson of the 2016 clip in miniature. Elena's
version of this exercise, for the student who has not opened a chatbot in a
year: this is ten minutes, it needs no skill with prompts, and the model
failing is the expected result, not your failure.

### Part B: your own forecast (15 minutes)

**Step 1. Find out how the time is actually spent.** The 36 percent figure for
radiology came from someone with a stopwatch. Most specialties have such a
study. Search PubMed with:

```
"time and motion studies"[MeSH] AND <your specialty>
```

adding `physician` or `resident` if the results are mostly about nurses.
Read the abstracts of the two most recent that observed physicians rather
than surveying them, and write down how the day divides. If your specialty
has no such study, say so on the sheet; that absence is itself a finding
about how well the job is understood, and you fall back on your own
sub-internship, honestly labeled as one observer's estimate.

**Step 2. Write three lines.**

```
Specialty: ____________________

1. The most automatable TASK in this specialty (a task, not the job):
   __________________________________________________________________

2. What fraction of the working day that task is, and where the number
   comes from (study / my own estimate):
   ______ %   source: ____________________________________________

3. The factor most likely to make my estimate wrong, and why:
   [ ] task decomposition  [ ] generalization  [ ] liability  [ ] demand
   __________________________________________________________________
```

Radiology's 36 percent is the benchmark on the screen, and most students
overestimate the fraction for their own field when they first write it down.
That is fine; the point of writing it down is to have something to be wrong
against later.

**Step 3. Attack it.** Reread your line 2 as the uncle at dinner. What would he
say is missing? Then reread it as the radiology resident in the second press
clipping. Change the number if either of them convinced you, and say which.

### Part C: close a flag yourself (10 minutes)

The module this chapter was built from carried the BLS projections marked
"unverified," because the government site blocked the automated fetch. You
are going to do what the software could not.

**Step 1.** Open the three BLS pages linked under @tbl-bls in your browser.
For each, find the "Job Outlook" section and record:

```
Occupation                          Projected change   Decade     BLS's stated reason
Medical transcriptionists           ______ %           ____–____  ___________________
Medical records specialists         ______ %           ____–____  ___________________
Health information technologists    ______ %           ____–____  ___________________
```

If your numbers differ from @tbl-bls, BLS has revised the projections since
this chapter was written. Note the new decade, and trust the page over the
chapter.

**Step 2.** In two sentences, explain why the first occupation moves one way
and the other two move the other, using at least two of the four factors by
name. Then one more sentence: who bears the cost of the −4 percent, and what
does that population look like compared with the +16 percent one?

## Check

Score yourself against this before moving on. Objective numbers refer to the
list at the top of the chapter.

| You have | Meets | Falls short |
|---|---|---|
| The prediction and its outcome (obj. 1) | You can state the 2016 claim, give two primary numbers from 2026 (positions, fill rate, or workforce projection), and say in one sentence why "early" is the wrong diagnosis | "He was wrong" with no number, or "he was just early" |
| A graded chatbot answer (obj. 2) | All four rows filled, and you searched PubMed for the study it cited | Rows ticked without checking anything |
| Your three-line forecast (obj. 2, 6) | A task, not a job; a fraction with a named source or an honest "my estimate"; a factor with a reason | "Documentation, 50%, probably fine" |
| The CAD sentence (obj. 3) | "Adoption and outcomes are separate questions," with the biopsy-rate finding attached | Only the slogan |
| The system-cost sentence (obj. 4) | You can explain in your own words why 5.8 percent more RVUs is not a cost reduction, and what "bot wars" means | "AI saves money" or "AI wastes money" without a mechanism |
| Three BLS rows (obj. 5) | Numbers and reasons read from the live pages, and a two-sentence explanation that names two factors | Numbers copied from this chapter |
| The "percent of what" habit | You can name the three denominators behind "25 percent administrative" | One number, one study |

## The standing question

*What does this change about how you'll practice, and what would you have to
see in the next five years to conclude you got this wrong?*

Write both halves down. For the first, go back to the dinner table: your uncle
is still holding his phone. What do you say about the 2016 quote, using one
number from this chapter and one of the four factors? If you are not going into
radiology, answer for your own specialty, with your Part B line 2 as the
number. For the second half, name the observation, a match statistic, a
workforce projection, a BLS revision, a change in who signs the report, that
would make you revise your forecast. A forecast with no possible refutation is
not a forecast; it is a mood.

Then keep the sheet from Part B. Reread it at the end of residency. Every
student who does this exercise has just made a confident forecast about a
medical specialty. So did a Nobel laureate, with better information than any
of you, and he got the mechanism wrong. The point of writing it down is to be
able to check.

## Summary

- The most confident job-elimination prediction in modern medicine has run its
  five-year course twice over. Radiology offered more positions in 2026 than
  ever, filled 98.4 percent of them, and projects a larger workforce in 2055.
- It failed on mechanism, not timing: a task was mistaken for a job. Four
  questions, task decomposition, generalization, liability, and demand,
  separate the two.
- Radiologists spend about a third of their time interpreting images. Most
  physician jobs decompose badly.
- Mammography CAD was adopted at scale, raised biopsies without raising cancer
  detection, made some readers worse, and was paid out of existence. Adoption
  and outcomes are separate questions.
- Scribes turn saved time into visits and RVUs. That is real and it is not
  cost reduction; across the system, administrative AI may be raising costs
  through bot wars.
- Transcription −4 percent, coding +8, health information +16, in the same
  department. The four factors explain the split, and the harm falls on the
  lowest-paid of the three.
- "Percent of what?" is a habit worth more than any of the three numbers.
- Your uncle, and your chatbot, are forecasting a job from a task. Now you can
  say why that is the mistake.

## Go deeper

**Papers**

- The time-and-motion study behind the 36 percent [@pmid:23763878], and the
  editorial that gave the field its slogan [@pmid:33937794].
- The two CAD studies [@pmid:17409321; @pmid:26414882] and the automation-bias
  experiment [@pmid:15354301], read together as one story.
- The generalization paper [@pmid:30399157], which is short and has a figure
  you will remember.
- The Neiman workforce papers: supply through 2055 [@pmid:39952776], attrition
  [@pmid:41031940], and the pediatric subspecialty [@pmid:40923948].
- The multi-society statement on buying and monitoring radiology AI
  [@pmid:38276923], which is what a department actually does with a cleared
  tool.
- The scribe economics: the five-system study [@pmid:41920565] and the UCSF
  productivity analysis [@pmid:41511775].
- The three administrative-cost papers [@pmid:31589283; @pmid:25201663;
  @pmid:12930930], for the denominators.

**Readings and talks**

- Deena Mousa, ["AI isn't replacing radiologists"](https://www.understandingai.org/p/ai-isnt-replacing-radiologists)
  (October 2025). The four-factor framework in this chapter is a compression
  of her argument.
- Peterson Health Technology Institute, [*Administrative AI: Current Use and
  Potential Impact*](https://phti.org/administrative-ai-current-use-and-potential-impact/)
  (April 2026), and KFF's interview with its director,
  ["The AI Arms Race in Administrative Health Care"](https://www.kff.org/other-health/the-ai-arms-race-in-administrative-health-care/)
  (July 2026).
- [A history of AI in medicine](https://talks.seandavis.net/archive/2025-09-30-ai-history/)
  carries the IBM Watson thread, Jeopardy! to MD Anderson setting it aside in
  2017, and MYCIN and the AI winters before it. Read it if you want a second
  instance of the same shape before deciding the Hinton story is about one
  man's bad call.
- [AI and machine learning for an oncology service line](https://talks.seandavis.net/archive/2024-10-28-ai-ml-oncology-service-line/)
  has the stakeholder framing, patients, providers, researchers,
  administrators, that the economics section needs, and the eight guiding
  principles [@doi:10.1038/s43856-023-00279-9], two of which, "have high
  healthcare value" and "reduce overdiagnosis and overtreatment," are the CAD
  story stated as rules.
